raw_case_text:
A 61-year-old Japanese man presented to the emergency department complaining of abdominal pain and loss of appetite. His medical history was significant for decompensated liver cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C: 11 points) due to nonalcoholic steatohepatitis, gastric varices treated with balloon-occluded retrograde transvenous obliteration and percutaneous transhepatic obliteration, hypertension, and diabetes mellitus. Medications included diuretics, branched-chain amino acid supplements, ursodeoxycholic acid, and a proton pump inhibitor.
Upon presentation, he had a fever of 38 C and was mildly tachycardic. Physical examination was significant for a distended abdomen with no tenderness and edema of the lower extremities. Laboratory data basically remained unchanged from his baseline, remarkable for serum albumin of 2.6 g/dL, creatinine of 1.11 mg/dL, total bilirubin of 7.9 mg/dL, sodium of 129 mEq/L, hemoglobin of 10.3 g/dL, platelet count of 106,000/mm3, white blood count of 10,000/mm3, C-reactive protein of 2.2 mg/dL, international normalized ratio of 1.27, and ammonia of 47 mumol/L. Serologic testing for HIV was negative. Paracentesis yielded clear ascites with minimal neutrophils. While cultures of blood and ascites (including fungi) were negative, intravenous antibiotics were given for suspected spontaneous bacterial peritonitis as no other cause of fever could be found. He was discharged 12 days later on oral antibiotics despite a persistent low-grade fever.
The patient was readmitted 8 days after discharge due to a high fever of 38.9 C. Weakness in the lower extremities and mild altered mental status were noted, initially believed to be due to hepatic encephalopathy, hyponatremia, or incipient sepsis. No meningeal signs were noted on physical examination. However, a new lump was observed in front of his right ear. The lump was soft and warm, but there was no tenderness. Ultrasonography of the right parotid gland revealed a 37.5 x 17.6 x 24.2 mm multilocular cystic lesion with clearly defined margins (Figure 1). Contrast CT of the neck revealed an enhancing multilocular cystic lesion in the right parotid gland (Figure 2). No masses, abscesses, or hydrocephalus were noted on contrast CT of the brain. Chest X-ray showed moderate pleural effusion limited to the right hemithorax. Fine-needle aspiration of the parotid lesion was performed, and 4 mL of yellow-green fluid was aspirated. Swelling and tenderness of the parotid gland resolved rapidly thereafter. Culture of the aspirate was positive for Cryptococcus neoformans.
Lumbar puncture revealed xanthochromic cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with an opening pressure of 22 cm H2O, a cell count of 100 cells/mm3 (39% neutrophils and 58% lymphocytes), pH of 8.0, protein of 109 mg/dl, and glucose of 20 mg/dl. Serum and CSF were both positive for the cryptococcal antigen, with a CSF titer of 1 : 8. India ink stain of CSF revealed an encapsulated yeast consistent with Cryptococcus neoformans. CSF culture was also positive for Cryptococcus neoformans. No growth was seen in blood, urine, and peritoneal fluid cultures. Upon detailed questioning, the patient stated that he worked in a fish market with frequent exposure to pigeons. CT with contrast showed multiple small low-attenuation areas in the spleen, suggestive of cryptococcal splenic abscesses (Figure 3(a)). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the spleen revealed multiple low-intensity areas more pronounced in the in-phase than in the opposed-phase on T1-weighted imaging (Figure 3(b)). A radiologist reviewed previous imaging studies and discovered multiple vague low-attenuation areas in the spleen on CT taken 4 months prior to admission. The patient was diagnosed with disseminated cryptococcosis.
The patient was started on liposomal amphotericin B and flucytosine. Lumbar puncture was repeated 11 days after commencing antifungal treatment, confirming negative CSF cultures for Cryptococcus neoformans. However, he died 23 days after admission and 17 days after the infection was confirmed. As repeated bacterial blood cultures remained negative and no other causes could be identified, disseminated cryptococcosis was determined to be the cause of death.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 61-year-old Japanese man with Child-Pugh class C nonalcoholic steatohepatitis cirrhosis presented with abdominal pain, anorexia, and fever, and was readmitted 8 days post-discharge with high fever (38.9 C), lower extremity weakness, mild altered mental status, and a new preauricular right parotid lump.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient initially presented with abdominal pain, loss of appetite, and fever (38 C) and was treated empirically for 12 days with antibiotics for suspected spontaneous bacterial peritonitis despite negative blood and ascitic fluid cultures. Eight days after discharge, he was readmitted with high fever (38.9 C), bilateral lower limb weakness, mild altered mental status, and a new painless, warm swelling in front of his right ear. He worked in a fish market with frequent exposure to pigeons.
subjective.past_medical_history: Decompensated liver cirrhosis (Child-Pugh C, 11 points) secondary to nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), gastric varices status post BRTO and PTO, hypertension, and diabetes mellitus. Fish market worker with frequent pigeon exposure.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for abdominal pain, anorexia, persistent fever, lower extremity weakness, mild confusion, and a right preauricular lump. Home medications: diuretics, branched-chain amino acids, ursodeoxycholic acid, and a proton-pump inhibitor.

objective.physical_examination: Initial admission: temperature 38 C, mild tachycardia, non-tender distended abdomen, and bilateral lower extremity edema. Readmission: temperature 38.9 C, mild altered mental status, lower extremity weakness, no meningeal irritation signs, and a soft, warm, non-tender right preauricular/parotid mass.
objective.routine_investigations: Albumin 2.6 g/dL, creatinine 1.11 mg/dL, total bilirubin 7.9 mg/dL, sodium 129 mEq/L, hemoglobin 10.3 g/dL, platelets 106,000/mm3, WBC 10,000/mm3, CRP 2.2 mg/dL, INR 1.27, ammonia 47 umol/L, and negative HIV serology. Blood, urine, and clear ascitic fluid cultures were negative; serum cryptococcal antigen was positive; chest X-ray on readmission showed a moderate right pleural effusion.
objective.advanced_workup: Right parotid ultrasound and contrast neck CT revealed a well-defined 37.5 x 17.6 x 24.2 mm enhancing multilocular cystic lesion in the right parotid gland; fine-needle aspiration yielded 4 mL of yellow-green fluid that grew Cryptococcus neoformans. Contrast head CT was normal, while contrast abdominal CT and splenic MRI identified multiple small hypodense/T1-hypointense splenic abscesses (retrospectively present on a CT 4 months prior). Lumbar puncture revealed xanthochromic CSF with opening pressure 22 cmH2O, WBC 100 cells/mm3 (58% lymphocytes, 39% neutrophils), pH 8.0, protein 109 mg/dL, glucose 20 mg/dL, positive CSF CrAg (titer 1:8), positive India ink stain, and CSF culture growing Cryptococcus neoformans.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis of fatal disseminated Cryptococcus neoformans infection presenting with right parotid gland abscess, splenic abscesses, and cryptococcal meningitis in a patient with Child-Pugh C NASH cirrhosis and occupational pigeon exposure, confirmed by right parotid aspirate culture, CSF India ink stain, positive serum and CSF CrAg (1:8), and positive CSF culture. Treated with parotid FNA drainage and IV liposomal amphotericin B plus flucytosine, achieving CSF culture sterilization by day 11 of antifungal therapy, but the patient died on hospital day 23 (17 days after confirmation) from complications of disseminated cryptococcosis and decompensated cirrhosis.
